title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection

headline_result.text: LLM-guided hybrid edits did not beat a matched random-policy hybrid (paired p = 0.612, 0.369, 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, 50), and a five-seed YOLO26m replication gave a mean official COCO AP change of +0.004 points (95% CI -0.026 to +0.034).

evidence_quality.n_runs_or_seeds: 1 to 5 seeds depending on budget (5 at B=8 and 25, 3 at B=50, 2 at B=100, 1 at B=250)

key_claims.claim: In the Phase III comparison, real LLM proposals gave smaller development gains than DE and CMA-ES; zero-shot LLM reached +0.03 development and -0.03 selection points.
Raising the CMA-ES budget to 250 evaluations increased development gains to +0.28 points while selection changes stayed negative (-0.12), consistent with selection overfitting; this row has one seed.
The five-seed YOLO26m replication produced a near-zero mean change on the selection images.
Of 225 archived LLM proposals, only 53 (23.6%) pass the final strict schema.
An earlier class labelled as LLM-guided only sampled Gaussian perturbations, so the author separates it from genuine LLM inference.

limitations_stated.quote: Observed development gains do not establish out-of-sample improvements.

notes_for_review: A careful negative study that applies WSP-style LLM edit proposals to YOLO26 detectors with a matched random-policy control and numerical optimizers (random search, DE, CMA-ES). All gains are hundredths of a point on development and vanish or turn negative on the selection set; the LLM adds no measurable benefit over the random policy. Weaknesses the author discloses: small local editor model (gemma4), few seeds, reused evaluation partitions, conflicting provenance for one subset, and an earlier Gaussian 'LLM' simulator that was mislabelled.
